mainTopic: Lashes for eating a טבל fig containing מעשר שני and the walls of ירושלים; then the משנה and ברייתא on קרחה, פאות, and שריטה for the dead.
overview: The amud opens by finishing a ברייתא in the name of רבי יוסי that counts the lashes for eating one fig that still has its gifts inside it. A כהן gets one set and a זר gets two. The גמרא infers that outside ירושלים there would be a third set for מעשר שני. That seems to contradict רבי יוחנן, who says there are lashes only once the produce 'saw the wall.' The answer is that the fig was brought into ירושלים and taken out. To explain what is new about that, the גמרא says the fig entered while still טבל, and רבי יוסי holds that unseparated gifts count as separated. A ברייתא about בית שמאי and בית הלל challenges this. רבה answers that the Torah wall for eating applies to טבל, while the rabbinic wall that 'captures' produce does not. רבינא instead says the fig was held on a reed, which would settle רב פפא's question. A new משנה then lists the bans on קרחה, rounding פאת הראש, destroying פאת הזקן, and שריטה for the dead, and counts how many liabilities each brings. The גמרא brings a ברייתא with the sources for קרחה and links כהנים and all Jews through a גזירה שוה. It then begins asking what case of 'four or five bald spots' is meant, a discussion that continues on the next amud.

steps.title: End of the ברייתא: one set of lashes for a כהן, two for a זר
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא finishes its count. A כהן who eats the fig gets one set of lashes, and a זר gets two. If the fig is eaten before anything was separated at all, the eater gets only one.
steps.simpleTranslation: [A כהן who eats it] is flogged once. A non-כהן who eats it is flogged twice. If he had eaten it at the very beginning, he would be flogged only once.
steps.whatsHappening: We are hearing the last lines of a ברייתא that counts how many sets of lashes a person gets for eating one fig that still contains its gifts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A כהן is allowed to eat תרומה, so his only problem is that the fig is still טבל, which gives one set of lashes. A זר is punished twice: once for טבל and once for eating the תרומה inside it. Before any separation was made, the fig is plain טבל, so there is only one set of lashes.

keyTerms.meaning: He is flogged (gets a set of מלקות).
A non-כהן, who is forbidden to eat תרומה.
At the beginning, before anything was separated from the produce.

phrases.english: is flogged once.
And a non-priest who ate it is flogged twice.
For had he eaten it at the start,
he would be flogged only once.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the ברייתא of רבי יוסי that started before this section.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A כהן gets one set of lashes (for טבל). A זר gets two (for טבל and for תרומה). Eaten before any separation, the fig brings only one.

steps.title: Outside ירושלים there would be three sets, even without seeing the wall
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא reads a hidden implication into the ברייתא. Outside ירושלים the eater would get a third set for מעשר שני, even though the fig never saw the city wall. That seems to contradict רבי יוחנן.
steps.simpleTranslation: The reason he gets only two is that he is in ירושלים. But in the outlying areas he would get three. So he is flogged even though the fig never saw the wall!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws an inference from the ברייתא and uses it to challenge רבי יוחנן's rule about מעשר שני.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Eating מעשר שני is allowed in ירושלים, so there the fig brings only two sets of lashes. Outside the city a third set would be added. Yet רבי יוחנן holds that you are flogged for eating מעשר שני outside only if it already 'saw the wall' of ירושלים, and here it apparently never did.

keyTerms.meaning: 'The reason is... but otherwise.' This is a pattern for drawing an inference from a source.
The outlying areas, outside ירושלים.
'Saw the face of the wall,' meaning the produce entered ירושלים.

steps.confusionAlert: The ברייתא never actually says 'three sets.' The גמרא is deducing it from the fact that the case is set in ירושלים.

phrases.english: The reason is that he is in Jerusalem,
but in the outlying areas he is flogged three times,

phrases.aramaic: דְּאַף עַל גַּב דְּלָאו רוֹאֶה פְּנֵי חוֹמָה!
phrases.english: so even though it did not see the face of the wall!
phrases.notes: This is aimed at רבי יוחנן, who requires that the produce entered ירושלים before there are lashes.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws an implication from the ברייתא just completed.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוחנן's rule that there are lashes for מעשר שני only after it 'saw the wall.'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא implies a third set of lashes outside ירושלים with no mention of the fig having entered the city.

steps.title: The fig was brought into ירושלים and taken out
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא is talking about a fig that entered ירושלים and was then taken out, so it did see the wall.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is a case where they brought it in and took it out.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רבי יוחנן by narrowing the case of the ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the fig already entered ירושלים, it has 'seen the wall.' Eating it outside afterwards fits רבי יוחנן's rule, so the third set of lashes is no contradiction.

keyTerms.meaning: They brought it in [to ירושלים] and took it out.

phrases.english: Where they brought it in and took it out.
phrases.notes: The letters in square brackets are the corrected wording, making it 'it,' meaning the fig.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 2.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא gives lashes outside ירושלים even without the fig seeing the wall.
steps.terutzMaskana: The fig had entered ירושלים and was taken out, so it did see the wall.

steps.title: If so, what is new about this?
steps.stepSummary: If the fig really entered ירושלים, lashes for eating it outside are obvious. Why did the ברייתא need to say it?
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, why say it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer it just gave: it seems to make the ברייתא teach nothing new.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Everyone agrees that מעשר שני which saw the wall and was taken out brings lashes when eaten outside. So the case would be pointless unless there is some new element in it.

keyTerms.meaning: If so.
What is there to say? Meaning, this is obvious.

phrases.english: If so, what is there to say?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer of step 3.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that the fig was brought in and taken out.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: That answer makes the ruling obvious, so it adds nothing.

steps.title: It entered while still טבל, and unseparated gifts count as separated
steps.stepSummary: The fig was brought into ירושלים while still טבל. The new point is that רבי יוסי treats gifts not yet separated as if they were already separated.
steps.simpleTranslation: What are we dealing with here? A case where he brought them in while they were still טבל, and he holds that gifts that were not separated are considered as if they were separated.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains what new point the ברייתא is teaching, which answers the question of step 4.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the fig entered ירושלים, its מעשר שני had not yet been separated. One might think it did not 'see the wall' as מעשר שני. Because רבי יוסי holds that gifts not yet separated are as if separated, the future מעשר שני portion already counts as having seen the wall.

keyTerms.meaning: 'What are we dealing with here?' This introduces a narrowed case.
Their state of טֶבֶל, produce whose gifts have not yet been taken.
The gifts: תרומה and the tithes.
Were separated (lifted off).
He holds (this view).

steps.whatToRemember: According to רבי יוסי, gifts not yet separated are treated as already separated. So a fig brought into ירושלים as טבל already counts as מעשר שני that saw the wall, and eating it outside brings lashes.
steps.whyThisMatters: This gives the ברייתא a real new point after step 3 had already saved רבי יוחנן's rule. Under רבי יוסי's view, gifts not yet separated count as if separated, even before the separation happens.

phrases.english: What are we dealing with here?
For example, where he brought them in while still untithed,
and he holds: gifts that were not separated
phrases.notes: 'He' is רבי יוסי, whose ברייתא this is.

phrases.english: are considered as if they were separated.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 4 by refining the case from step 3.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case further and identifying the view it rests on
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Bringing the fig in and taking it out is an obvious case, with nothing new.
steps.terutzMaskana: It entered as טבל, and the new point is that unseparated gifts count as separated, so its מעשר שני saw the wall.

steps.title: A ברייתא from רבי יוסי seems to say the opposite
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether רבי יוסי really holds that unseparated gifts count as separated. It quotes a ברייתא in his name about produce that passed through ירושלים.
steps.simpleTranslation: Does רבי יוסי really hold that unseparated gifts are like separated ones? A ברייתא in his name says: בית שמאי and בית הלל agree that produce whose work was not finished, and which passed through ירושלים, may have its מעשר שני redeemed and eaten anywhere. They argue about produce whose work was finished and then passed through ירושלים. בית שמאי say the מעשר שני must be brought back and eaten in ירושלים. בית הלל say it may be redeemed and eaten anywhere.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the last answer by quoting a ברייתא in רבי יוסי's name. This step lays out the ברייתא, and the next step will show why it creates a problem.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 5 said רבי יוסי treats unseparated gifts as if they were already separated. Here, בית הלל let produce that passed through ירושלים before separating be redeemed outside. That suggests the מעשר שני inside it was not yet 'real' while it was in the city.

keyTerms.meaning: Gifts (like תרומה and מעשר) that have not yet been separated from the produce
The produce's processing is finished, so the obligation to tithe now applies
Redeeming: moving the holiness of מעשר שני onto money so the food can be eaten anywhere

steps.confusionAlert: Both cases in the ברייתא involve produce that passed through ירושלים before anything was separated. The only difference is whether the produce was already finished and obligated in tithes.

phrases.english: And does Rabbi Yosei hold
that gifts that were not separated
are like ones that were separated?
But isn't it taught in a ברייתא:

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי יוֹסֵי:
phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda says in the name of Rabbi Yosei:

phrases.aramaic: לֹא נֶחְלְקוּ בֵּית שַׁמַּאי וּבֵית הִלֵּל
phrases.english: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel did not disagree
about produce whose work was not yet finished
and which passed through Jerusalem,
that its second tithe may be redeemed
and eaten anywhere.
And about what did they disagree?
About produce whose work was finished
and which passed through Jerusalem,
for Beit Shammai say:
he must bring its second tithe back
and it is eaten in Jerusalem,
and Beit Hillel say:
it may be redeemed and eaten anywhere.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְסָבַר רַבִּי יוֹסֵי מַתָּנוֹת שֶׁלֹּא הוּרְמוּ כְּמִי שֶׁהוּרְמוּ דָּמֵי? וְהָתַנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 5 by quoting a ברייתא from רבי יוסי himself.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that רבי יוסי treats unseparated gifts as already separated.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי יוסי reports that בית הלל let such produce be redeemed outside ירושלים. That fits better with treating the unseparated מעשר שני as not yet real.

steps.title: The punchline: the walls should have captured it
steps.stepSummary: If unseparated gifts counted as separated, the produce in בית הלל's case would already be 'captured' by the walls of ירושלים and could not be redeemed.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you think unseparated gifts are like separated ones, then the walls of ירושלים already captured this produce!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the challenge. It shows how the ברייתא contradicts the answer from step 5.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once מעשר שני enters ירושלים, it normally may not be redeemed or taken out. If the unseparated tithe already counted as tithe, בית הלל could not allow redeeming it. So רבי יוסי, who follows בית הלל, must not treat unseparated gifts as separated.

keyTerms.meaning: The walls of ירושלים 'captured' it, so the מעשר שני can no longer be redeemed or taken out
And if it enters your mind: a phrase that sets up an idea in order to reject it

phrases.english: And if it enters your mind
that gifts not yet separated
are like ones that were separated,
the walls already captured it!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי סָלְקָא דַעְתָּךְ מַתָּנוֹת שֶׁלֹּא הוּרְמוּ כְּמִי שֶׁהוּרְמוּ דָּמְיָין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the contradiction out of the ברייתא quoted in step 6.
steps.kashyaTarget: Step 5's claim that רבי יוסי holds unseparated gifts count as separated.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Under that view, the walls would capture the produce and block redemption. Yet בית הלל allow redemption.

steps.title: רבה: two different wall laws
steps.stepSummary: רבה splits the wall into two laws. Not eating outside the wall is from the Torah. The wall capturing produce is from the רבנן, who did not apply it to טבל.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said: the wall's law about eating is from the Torah. The wall's law about capturing is from the רבנן. When the רבנן made their decree, it was only for tithe that is already separate and standing on its own. For produce that is still טבל, the רבנן did not make the decree.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה defends step 5 by showing that the ברייתא does not really contradict it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Lashes for eating מעשר שני outside the wall come from the Torah, and for that רבי יוסי can treat unseparated gifts as separated. The rule that the wall 'captures' produce and blocks redemption is only from the רבנן. They never applied it to טבל, so בית הלל can allow redemption without contradicting רבי יוסי's view.

keyTerms.meaning: The wall as a limit for eating: מעשר שני may not be eaten outside ירושלים
The wall as something that captures: once inside, the produce may not be redeemed or taken out
From the Torah
From the רבנן (a rabbinic law)
In its own form: tithe that is already separate
Produce from which the required gifts have not yet been separated

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that a Torah law and a rabbinic law about the same wall can follow different rules. That lets both ברייתות stand.

phrases.english: Rabbah said:
The wall for eating is from the Torah;
the wall for capturing is rabbinic.
And when the Rabbis decreed,
it was when it exists in its own form;
phrases.notes: He means the מעשר שני has already been separated and stands on its own.

phrases.english: while still טבל, the Rabbis did not decree.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of steps 6–7 and keeps step 5's answer alive.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing two laws: the Torah eating wall and the rabbinic capturing wall
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought the wall either takes hold of טבל for everything or for nothing.
steps.terutzMaskana: For the Torah ban on eating, unseparated tithe counts. The rabbinic capturing rule does not apply to טבל, so בית הלל can allow redemption.

steps.title: רבינא: the fig was held on a reed
steps.stepSummary: רבינא explains the ברייתא differently. The case is a fig held on a reed, so it is not about טבל at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said: the case is where he holds the fig on a reed.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא offers another way to explain the original ברייתא. This removes the need for the טבל explanation of step 5.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Instead of saying the fig entered ירושלים as טבל, רבינא says the fig was already separated מעשר שני. It reached the wall only by being held on a reed. The new point of the ברייתא is that even this counts as the fig having 'seen the wall,' so eating it outside brings lashes.

keyTerms.meaning: A reed or stick used to hold the fruit
Holds

steps.confusionAlert: רבינא is not adding to רבה's answer. He gives a completely different reason why the ברייתא needed to tell us this case.

phrases.english: Ravina said:
For example, where he holds it on a reed.
phrases.notes: The person stands inside ירושלים, and the fig on the reed sticks out beyond the wall.

steps.triggerLanguage: רָבִינָא אָמַר: כְּגוֹן דְּנָקֵיט לֵיהּ בְּקַנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a different answer to the question of step 4 (why the ברייתא needed to teach this), instead of the טבל answer.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought the only new point possible was the טבל case.
steps.terutzMaskana: The new point is that a fig held on a reed counts as having seen the wall.

steps.title: This settles רב פפא's question
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא notes that רבינא's answer would settle רב פפא's earlier question about produce held on a reed.
steps.simpleTranslation: And then you can settle רב פפא's question.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out a side result of רבינא's explanation. It also answers a question רב פפא left open.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב פפא had asked whether produce held on a reed counts as having entered ירושלים. If רבינא is right that the ברייתא is about a reed, then the ברייתא shows that it does count.

keyTerms.meaning: Resolve, settle (an open question)
An open question left without an answer

steps.whatToRemember: There are two ways to explain the new point of רבי יוסי's ruling. In the first, the fig entered as טבל and unseparated gifts count as separated. רבה defends this against the בית שמאי and בית הלל ברייתא: the Torah eating-wall applies to טבל, but the rabbinic capturing-wall does not. In the second, רבינא says the case is a fig held on a reed, which would settle רב פפא's question.

phrases.english: And resolve the question of Rav Pappa.
phrases.notes: This is the question on the previous daf about whether a reed counts for entering ירושלים.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws a consequence from רבינא's answer.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: According to רבינא, produce held on a reed counts as having entered ירושלים, which answers רב פפא's question.

steps.title: Four forbidden acts and counting cuts for the dead
steps.stepSummary: The משנה lists four acts that bring lashes: קרחה, rounding פאת הראש, destroying פאת הזקן, and a שריטה for the dead. Each separate cut brings its own liability.
steps.simpleTranslation: Someone who makes a bald spot on his head, rounds the edge of his head, destroys the edge of his beard, or makes one cut on his skin for a dead person is liable. If he made one cut for five dead people, or five cuts for one dead person, he is liable for each one.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה opens. It lists four acts that bring lashes and says that cuts for the dead are counted one by one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even a single שריטה is enough for liability. The משנה then shows two ways to multiply the count: one cut that is for five different dead people, or five cuts for one dead person. Either way, each counts as a separate liability.

keyTerms.meaning: A bald spot made on the head, usually by pulling out hair, as a sign of mourning
The edge of the head, the hair near the ears
The edge or corner of the beard
A cut or scratch in the skin made in mourning for the dead
Liable, here meaning he gets lashes

phrases.english: MISHNA: One who makes a bald spot on his head
and one who rounds the edge of his head,
phrases.notes: This means shaving the hair next to the ear so the hairline looks rounded.

phrases.english: and one who destroys the edge of his beard,

phrases.aramaic: וְהַשּׂוֹרֵט שְׂרִיטָה אַחַת עַל הַמֵּת – חַיָּיב.
phrases.english: and one who cuts one cut over the dead, is liable.

phrases.aramaic: שָׂרַט שְׂרִיטָה אַחַת עַל חֲמִשָּׁה מֵתִים,
phrases.english: If he cut one cut over five dead people,

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ חָמֵשׁ שְׂרִיטוֹת עַל מֵת אֶחָד –
phrases.english: or five cuts over one dead person,
he is liable for each and every one.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new משנה with a new topic, unrelated to the previous discussion about טבל and the walls of ירושלים.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: קרחה, rounding פאת הראש, destroying פאת הזקן, and a single שריטה for the dead each bring lashes. Multiple dead people or multiple cuts multiply the liability.

steps.title: How many edges on the head and the beard
steps.stepSummary: The head has two edges and the beard has five, each a separate liability. רבי אליעזר says that if all are removed at once, there is only one liability.
steps.simpleTranslation: For the head there are two edges, one on each side. For the beard there are two on each side and one below. רבי אליעזר says: if all of them were removed in one action, he is liable only once.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה counts how many separate liabilities there can be for the edges of the head and the beard. רבי אליעזר disagrees when everything is removed in one action.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first opinion counts by place: two edges on the head and five on the beard, so each removed edge is its own liability. רבי אליעזר counts by action: if one act removed all the edges together, it is only one liability.

keyTerms.meaning: From here and from here, meaning on both sides
From below, the chin area
At once, in one action

phrases.english: On the head, two,
one from here and one from here,

phrases.aramaic: עַל הַזָּקָן – שְׁתַּיִם מִכָּאן וּשְׁתַּיִם מִכָּאן,
phrases.english: on the beard, two from here and two from here,
and one from below.
Rabbi Eliezer says:
If they were all removed at once,
he is liable only for one.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה, now counting liabilities for the edges of the head and beard.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: First opinion: two liabilities for the head and five for the beard. רבי אליעזר: one action removing all of them brings only one liability.

steps.title: Only a razor, or also tweezers and a plane
steps.stepSummary: The first opinion says one is liable for the beard only with a razor. רבי אליעזר says tweezers or a plane also make one liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: He is not liable unless he removes the hair with a razor. רבי אליעזר says: even if he plucked it with tweezers or with a plane, he is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה ends with a dispute about which tools make a person liable for destroying the beard.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to the first opinion, only a תער, which cuts the hair right at the skin, makes one liable. רבי אליעזר widens it to other tools that also remove the hair completely, like tweezers or a plane.

keyTerms.meaning: A razor
Tweezers, a tool for plucking hairs
A plane, a smoothing tool used by carpenters

phrases.english: And he is not liable unless he removes it with a razor.
Rabbi Eliezer says:
Even if he plucked it with tweezers
or with a plane, he is liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה with the question of which tool brings liability.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: First opinion: liability for the beard only with a razor. רבי אליעזר: tweezers or a plane also make one liable.
steps.whatToRemember: The משנה has three parts: (1) four forbidden acts, with each cut counted separately; (2) two edges on the head and five on the beard, where רבי אליעזר says one action is one liability; (3) a razor only, where רבי אליעזר says tweezers and a plane also count.

steps.title: Each bald spot is its own liability
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא learns from the singular word קרחה that one is liable for every single bald spot, even if he made several.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: "They shall not make bald." I might think that even if he made four or five bald spots, he is liable only once. So the verse says "a bald spot," to make him liable for each and every bald spot.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins with a ברייתא that finds a source for counting each bald spot separately.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One might think that one prohibition means only one liability, however many bald spots he made. The ברייתא points to the word קרחה in the singular. Each single bald spot is what the Torah forbids, so each one counts on its own.

keyTerms.meaning: I might have thought, which introduces a wrong first assumption
The verse comes to teach, which introduces the answer from the פסוק
Each and every bald spot

phrases.english: GEMARA: The Sages taught: "They shall not make bald,"
one might think that even if he made bald
four or five bald spots
he would be liable only once?
The verse says "a bald spot,"
phrases.notes: The word is singular, so the point is that each single bald spot is a separate sin.

phrases.english: to make him liable for each and every bald spot.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The גמרא brings a ברייתא with the Torah source for the משנה's idea that one can be liable many times over.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: From the singular קרחה, one is liable separately for every bald spot.

steps.title: Why does the verse add the word 'on their head'
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא asks what the word בראשם adds. Another פסוק mentions a bald spot 'between your eyes,' so one might think only that spot is forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why does the verse say "on their head"? Because another verse says, "Do not cut yourselves, and do not place a bald spot between your eyes for the dead." I might think he is liable only for the area between the eyes. From where do we learn that the whole head is included?
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא asks why the word בראשם is needed. It sets up the problem by quoting a different פסוק that seems to limit the prohibition to the space between the eyes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק in דברים says בין עיניכם, between your eyes. Read alone, it sounds like only a bald spot in the front of the head is forbidden. The question is where we learn that the rest of the head is included, and this prepares the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: What does the verse come to teach, asking why a word is needed
Do not cut yourselves, a mourning practice the Torah forbids
Between your eyes, the front of the head above the forehead
From where do we know

steps.confusionAlert: There are two different פסוקים here. "On their head" comes from ויקרא 21:5, and "between your eyes" comes from דברים 14:1. The ברייתא uses the first one to widen the second.

phrases.english: "On their head": why does the verse say this?
Since it says
"You shall not cut yourselves
and you shall not place a bald spot
between your eyes for the dead,"
one might think he would not be liable
except for between the eyes alone.
From where do we include the whole head?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא, now explaining the next word in the פסוק.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why is the word בראשם needed, and what is the source that a bald spot anywhere on the head is forbidden, not only between the eyes?

steps.title: The word 'on their head' includes the whole head
steps.stepSummary: The word בראשם teaches that a bald spot anywhere on the head is forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: The verse says "on their head," to include the whole head.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא answers its own question: בראשם widens the prohibition to the entire head.
steps.deeperAnalysis: "Between your eyes" by itself could sound like a limit. The word בראשם shows that the whole head is included, so a bald spot anywhere on the head brings liability.

keyTerms.meaning: To include, adding cases beyond the simple reading

steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא learns two things from the פסוק: from קרחה (singular), each bald spot is a separate liability; from בראשם, the whole head is included, not only between the eyes.

phrases.english: The verse says "on their head,"
to include the whole head.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question raised in the previous step.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The word בראשם is needed to include the entire head in the prohibition of קרחה.

steps.title: Where do we learn this for a regular Jew?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא notes that the bald-spot rules so far were learned from a פסוק about כהנים, and asks where we learn them for a regular Jew.
steps.simpleTranslation: So far we only know this about כהנים, and the Torah gave כהנים extra מצוות. Where do we learn it for a regular Jew?
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא asks a question. The rules it just learned (liability for each bald spot, and for a bald spot anywhere on the head) came from a פסוק about כהנים, so how do we know they apply to every Jew?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since כהנים have extra מצוות that regular Jews do not, we cannot just assume their rules carry over to everyone. So the ברייתא needs a separate source for a regular Jew. This sets up the next step's answer.

keyTerms.meaning: Extra מצוות. These are additional commandments given only to כהנים.
Here it means a regular Jew who is not a כהן.
From where? It asks for a source.

phrases.english: And I have this only for priests,
phrases.notes: The rules from steps 14 to 16 were learned from the פסוק about כהנים in ויקרא 21:5.

phrases.english: for whom the Torah gave extra מצוות,
from where do we know it for a regular Jew?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After learning the כהנים rules from the פסוק, the ברייתא asks how they extend to all Jews.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A source showing that a regular Jew has the same bald-spot rules as a כהן.

steps.title: Linking the two verses through the shared word קרחה
steps.stepSummary: A גזירה שוה on the word קרחה makes the rules for כהנים and for all Jews match, in both directions.
steps.simpleTranslation: The word 'bald spot' appears here and there. Just as there one is liable for each bald spot, and for anywhere on the head just like between the eyes, so too here. And just as there it is about mourning for the dead, so too here it is about the dead.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא answers with a גזירה שוה: both פסוקים use the word קרחה, so their laws are shared.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two rules pass from the כהנים verse to all Jews: you are liable for each separate bald spot, and the whole head counts, not just 'between the eyes.' In return, the detail 'for the dead,' which appears only in the verse about all Jews, passes to the כהנים. So the link works both ways.

keyTerms.meaning: A teaching that links two פסוקים because they share the same word, so the laws of one apply to the other.
'It says here... and it says there.' This is the standard opening of a גזירה שוה.
Between the eyes. This is the place the פסוק for all Jews mentions.
For a dead person. The bald spot is forbidden when made as mourning.

steps.whatToRemember: The rules of קרחה are the same for כהנים and for all Jews: you are liable for each bald spot, anywhere on the head, when it is made in mourning for the dead.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that a גזירה שוה can carry details in both directions, so each verse fills in what the other leaves out.

phrases.english: 'Bald spot' is said here
phrases.notes: 'Here' is the פסוק about all Jews, דברים 14:1.

phrases.english: and 'bald spot' is said there,
phrases.notes: 'There' is the פסוק about כהנים, ויקרא 21:5.

phrases.aramaic: מָה לְהַלָּן חַיָּיב עַל כׇּל קׇרְחָה וְקׇרְחָה,
phrases.english: just as there one is liable for each and every bald spot,
and is liable for the head just as for between the eyes,

phrases.aramaic: אַף כָּאן חַיָּיב עַל כׇּל קׇרְחָה וְקׇרְחָה,
phrases.english: so too here one is liable for each and every bald spot,
and is liable for the head just as for between the eyes.
And just as there it is for the dead,
phrases.notes: Here the direction flips. 'For the dead' is written in the verse for all Jews, and it gets carried over to the כהנים.

phrases.english: so too here it is for the dead.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 17.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A גזירה שוה on the word קרחה applies the כהנים rules to all Jews, and the 'for the dead' detail to כהנים.

steps.title: What case of four or five bald spots is meant?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what exact situation the 'four or five bald spots' case is talking about.
steps.simpleTranslation: These four or five bald spots, what is the case?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new question about the case of someone who made several bald spots. This sets up a search for the exact situation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We know each bald spot brings its own liability. Now the גמרא wants to pin down how the spots were made, so that the ruling actually teaches something new.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? It asks for the exact situation.
Bald spots. This is the plural of קרחה.

phrases.english: These four or five bald spots,
what is the case?

steps.triggerLanguage: הָנֵי אַרְבַּע וְחָמֵשׁ קְרִיחוֹת הֵיכִי דָמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from finding the source to defining the case of several bald spots.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The exact situation in which someone gets several liabilities for several bald spots.

steps.title: Separate acts with separate warnings is too obvious
steps.stepSummary: The first suggestion, that he made the bald spots one after another with five warnings, is rejected as obvious.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say it was one after the other, with five warnings, that is obvious!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries a first answer and immediately pushes it away, because that case would not need to be taught.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If each bald spot was a separate act with its own warning, then of course each one is punished separately. Saying so teaches nothing new. So the case must be something less obvious, which the גמרא will look for next.

keyTerms.meaning: If you say. This introduces a suggestion that will be tested.
One after the other, as separate acts.
A warning given before the sin. It is needed before someone can get lashes.
It's obvious! This means there is no need to teach it.

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the גמרא is saying he is not liable in this case. He is liable for each spot. The point is only that this case is too obvious to be what is meant.

phrases.english: If you say it was one after the other,
and with five warnings,
that is obvious!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִילֵּימָא בְּזֶה אַחַר זֶה, וּבְחָמֵשׁ הַתְרָאוֹת – פְּשִׁיטָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries a first answer to step 19 and rejects it.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects reading the case as separate acts, each with its own warning.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: That case is obviously liable for each spot, so it would teach nothing new.
